bib.title: Computer Age Statistical Inference, Chapter 1: Algorithms and Inference

question: How do the algorithmic and inferential halves of statistical analysis divide the work, and how did computers change both?
contributions: Separates algorithm (what the statistician does) from inference (why, and how accurate it is).
Two worked previews of classic versus computer-age practice: kidney-function regression (estimation) and leukemia gene testing (hypothesis testing).

results.claim: Least squares on 157 volunteers gives intercept 2.86 for kidney function tot against age.
results.setup: Kidney data, n=157 healthy volunteers, x=age, y=composite function measure tot, linear fit y = b0 + b1 x by least squares.
results.note: Slope printed as minus 0.079 (minus sign lost in text extraction).

results.claim: Least squares slope for tot against age is -0.079 per year.
results.setup: Same linear fit to kidney data.

results.claim: Linear-regression standard error is smallest (.15) at ages 30-40 and largest (.42) at age 80; the +/-2 SE bars give about 95% coverage if the linear model is valid.
results.table: Table 1.1, row 2. std error, column age 80
results.note: Coverage statement: 'about 95% chance of containing the true expected value of tot at each age', conditional on the linear model.

results.claim: Lowess(x,y,1/3) bootstrap standard errors are roughly double those of linear regression, the price of flexibility.
results.setup: Kidney data; bootstrap = resample 157 (x,y) pairs with replacement, rerun lowess; 250 replications; bootstrap SEs at ages 20..80: .71 .23 .31 .32 .37 .47 .70 versus .21 .15 .15 .19 .26 .34 .42 for linear.
results.table: Table 1.1, row 4. bootstrap std error, column age 80 (and row 2 for baseline)

results.claim: The bootstrap assesses accuracy for any algorithm at a hundred- or thousand-fold increase in computation.
results.setup: General statement in Sec 1.1; example uses the first 25 of 250 replications in Fig 1.3.

results.claim: Lowess shows the curve flat between ages 25 and 35, unlike the uniform decline of the linear fit.
results.setup: Kidney data, lowess(x,y,1/3), local polynomial fit with repeated robustness passes.

results.claim: Gene 136: two-sample t = 3.01 on 70 df, two-sided p = 0.0036; group means 0.752 (ALL) and 0.950 (AML).
results.setup: Leukemia data: 47 ALL and 25 AML patients, 7,128 genes; t = (mean AML - mean ALL)/sd-hat, Student t null with 70 df (Gaussian assumptions).
results.note: p-value printed .0036 in Fig 1.4 caption and 0.0036 in text.

results.claim: Across all 7128 genes about 400 others exceed t = 3.01 (5.6%), so gene 136 is not significant at the 0.056 level and the p-value 0.0036 overstates the evidence.
results.setup: Same leukemia data; multiplicity (7128 candidates) plus a theoretical null that is much too narrow at the centre.

results.claim: A low false-discovery rate requires t exceeding 6.16, which only 47 of 7128 genes meet.
results.setup: ALL/AML study; derived in Chapter 15 (not shown here).
results.note: Forward reference to Ch. 15; method not derived in this chapter.

results.claim: Averaging is the algorithm; the standard error is the inference about its accuracy, computed from the same data.
results.setup: Eq 1.1 mean; Eq 1.2 se-hat = [sum (x_i - xbar)^2 / (n(n-1))]^(1/2); example n=50 states' accident rates.

limits: Preview chapter: methods (bootstrap, FDR, empirical Bayes, lowess) are only named and deferred to Ch. 6, 8, 10, 15, 17.
Single dataset per example, no repeated-sample check of the 95% coverage claim; coverage is conditional on the linear model.
The 6.16 FDR threshold is asserted with no derivation here.
Authors say the book is about an evolution, not a revolution, in inference; a golden age for methodology but not quite for inference.
practices: Report every estimate with its standard error; the same data can supply both (p.3).
When a model assumption (linearity) drives coverage, check it with a more flexible fit such as quadratic, cubic or lowess (p.5-6).
For algorithms with no accuracy formula, use the bootstrap: resample the n pairs with replacement, rerun the algorithm, take the standard deviation of replications (p.7).
With thousands of simultaneous tests, do not read a single p-value at face value; use false-discovery-rate control (p.9).
Check the theoretical null against the histogram of test statistics; here it is too narrow at the centre (p.9).
